candidates.attacker_control: A remote, unauthenticated request to /realms/{realm}/protocol/openid-connect/auth (GET) or the authorization endpoint (POST) supplying client_id of any enabled client plus an arbitrary request_uri value (e.g. http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/, http://127.0.0.1:8080/admin, http://internal-host:port/). No cookies, tokens or client secrets are required; public client_ids are typically enumerable/published (login URL, account console, security-admin-console).
candidates.counterevidence_checked: Checked that the authorization endpoint still runs checkSsl/checkRealm/checkClient before parsing (so an enabled client_id is needed) and that the response is parsed as a JWS and errors are generic. Checked that no scheme check, host allow-list, or use of the client's registered request_uris exists anywhere in the snapshot (only the unused OIDCClientRepresentation.getRequestUris field). Verified HttpClientProvider.get has no URL restrictions and follows default redirect behavior; verified StreamUtil.readString is unbounded. Considered that OIDC request_uri fetching is spec-permitted, but the absence of any registration/allow-list or private-address blocking is what makes it unsafe here. Version tag 4.6.0.Final-SNAPSHOT is consistent with this code base being older than later fixes for request_uri SSRF; exact CVE/commit attribution could not be verified from the snapshot (no git metadata, no tests, no release notes).
candidates.impact: Server-side request forgery from the Keycloak server: internal network/service reachability and port probing (loopback, RFC1918, link-local/cloud metadata endpoints), ability to trigger side-effecting GET endpoints on internal systems, and potential denial of service by pointing request_uri at an endpoint/large or slowly-streaming response that is read unbounded into memory (StreamUtil.readString). It can also be combined with Keycloak's own internal/admin (localhost-bound) endpoints. No direct file read or RCE is demonstrated by this path.
candidates.prerequisites: Keycloak server reachable by the attacker; at least one enabled client in the realm (default realm installations contain several); client attribute `request.object.required` not set to a value that forbids request_uri (default is 'not required'); network path from the Keycloak server to the chosen URL (typical for internal SSRF). The attacker does not receive the response body, so the impact is blind SSRF/DoS rather than direct data disclosure.
candidates.root_cause: In AuthorizationEndpointRequestParserProcessor.parseRequest, the attacker-supplied OIDC `request_uri` query/form parameter (OIDCLoginProtocol.REQUEST_URI_PARAM) is passed verbatim to `session.getProvider(HttpClientProvider.class).get(requestUriParam)`. There is no validation that the URL is HTTPS, that its host is registered for the client (the OIDCClientRepresentation.request_uris value is never consumed anywhere in the server), or that it does not target loopback/link-local/internal addresses. The default client setting `request.object.required` is unset (treated as 'not required'), so any enabled client (including a public client whose client_id is public) can be used. The response stream is then read with no size limit (StreamUtil.readString) before being parsed as a JWS request object, and the parse failure is reported as a generic invalid_request, leaving a blind SSRF. The outbound client itself performs a plain HttpGet with a shared connection pool and default redirect handling (DefaultHttpClientFactory.get).
candidates.title: Unauthenticated SSRF via OIDC authorization endpoint `request_uri` parameter
candidates.trace:
1) AuthorizationEndpoint.process() (lines 111-118) resolves the realm/client and calls AuthorizationEndpointRequestParserProcessor.parseRequest() after only checkSsl/checkRealm/checkClient (no authentication).
2) parseRequest() (lines 48-49) extracts the raw `request_uri` parameter.
3) Lines 70-75: when `request_uri` is present (and `request` is not), the server invokes HttpClientProvider.get(requestUriParam) and drains the response into a String with no length bound; only afterwards is the content parsed as a JWS request object.
4) DefaultHttpClientFactory.get() (lines 100-107) executes an Apache HttpClient HttpGet against the attacker-chosen URI using the server's pooled outbound client (proxy mappings only if configured).
5) Any fetch/parse error is collapsed into Messages.INVALID_REQUEST (lines 80-84), so the exchange is blind to the attacker but the internal request has already been issued.
candidates.unverified: Not runtime-confirmed. Whether this specific path is the planted/known issue for this case is unverified; the code, source-to-sink trace and absence of validation are confirmed by reading. Impact severity depends on deployment/network topology (proxy mappings, truststore, firewall). External request via HttpClient could not be executed in this read-only review.
candidates.weakness_type: Server-Side Request Forgery (CWE-918), unvalidated URL fetch by server

coverage_summary: Coverage is partial and source-driven. I started with get_source_scope (5,108 model-visible files, no binary/symlink/sensitive-name exclusions reported) and used repository-wide literal searches for common vulnerability sinks (command execution, deserialization, SQL/JPQL concatenation, XML/StAX/DOM parser creation, trust managers/hostname verifiers, redirects, path handling, random/password hashing, authorization/role checks, XSS-prone admin JS), then read the relevant files. Files inspected in detail include services OIDC endpoints (AuthorizationEndpoint, AuthorizationEndpointRequestParserProcessor, AuthzEndpointRequestObjectParser, LogoutEndpoint, TokenEndpoint/TokenManager), ClientRegistrationAuth/policies, IdentityBrokerService, SAMLEndpoint, AuthenticationManager/ClientSessionCode/CodeGenerateUtil, Pbkdf2PasswordHashProvider, admin permission evaluators, saml-core DocumentUtil/StAX/XMLSignatureUtil/AssertionUtil, the three HttpClientBuilder copies, keycloak.js, admin themes JS, and numerous utility classes. Notably, the tool-visible tree contains no `.ftl` templates and no `src/test` sources, and there is no `.git` metadata, so template-rendered output and test-implied behavior could not be inspected and no commit history/diff against upstream was available.
limitations: No precomputed source-relation index in this B0 run; all tracing was manual text search/reading of 5,108 files, so most files were not read line-by-line.
Read-only review only: nothing was compiled, executed, or fuzzed; findings are not runtime-confirmed and no external request was made.
The visible snapshot omits .ftl templates and test sources. Vulnerabilities that manifest only in theme templates or would be revealed by regression tests cannot be inspected or confirmed here.

No VCS metadata/diff/patches are present, so the exact upstream revision and any planted/known-issue mapping (e.g., CVE/commit attribution such as the known request_uri SSRF advisories) could not be verified; the candidate is a source-evidenced lead, not a confirmed match.
The outbound client's effective behavior depends on deployment configuration (proxy-mappings, truststore, firewall/DNS); the SSRF reachability and impact therefore vary per installation.

Only one candidate is permitted; several plausible but weaker/unconfirmed leads (sector_identifier_uri SSRF, certificate CRL-distribution-point fetch, admin-console HTML injection, StAX entity handling) are recorded as rejected leads rather than separate candidates.

rejected_leads.lead: SSRF via OIDC sector_identifier_uri: PairwiseSubMapperValidator.getSectorRedirects() fetches a client-supplied sector_identifier_uri through HttpClientProvider (services/src/main/java/org/keycloak/protocol/oidc/utils/PairwiseSubMapperValidator.java lines 84-109), and the HTTPS scheme check in PairwiseSubMapperUtils.resolveValidSectorIdentifier (lines 63-78) is commented out. Rejected as the single candidate because the reachable paths (client create/update through admin REST or client registration) require authenticated admin/client-registration privileges, making attacker control weaker than the unauthenticated request_uri path.
rejected_leads.reason: Requires privileged/registered caller; weaker attacker model than the selected candidate.

rejected_leads.lead: SSRF/URL fetch in X.509 authenticator CRL handling: CertificateValidator loads CRL distribution-point URIs embedded in a client-presented certificate (services/src/main/java/org/keycloak/authentication/authenticators/x509/CertificateValidator.java lines 249-263, 488-497). Rejected: requires the X.509 client-certificate authenticator to be enabled with CRL checking configured, so it is not reachable in a default deployment.
rejected_leads.reason: Non-default configuration needed; not the strongest reachable issue.

rejected_leads.lead: Stored/DOM XSS in the admin console authorization-services dialog: AuthzDialog.openDialog uses $sce.trustAsHtml(message) and confirmDelete interpolates an unescaped name into that message (themes/src/main/resources/theme/base/admin/resources/js/authz/authz-services.js lines 81-131) while the generic services.js dialog has an escapeHtml helper. Rejected as an unconfirmed hardening gap: it requires a user able to create authorization resources/policies (already privileged) and I could not confirm the exact escaping behavior of the upstream revision.
rejected_leads.reason: Privileged attacker and unverified upstream diff; not selected.

rejected_leads.lead: SAML StAX parser entity handling: StaxParserUtil sets XMLInputFactory.IS_REPLACING_ENTITY_REFERENCES to TRUE (saml-core/.../StaxParserUtil.java lines 874-879) with SUPPORT_DTD not explicitly disabled, while IS_SUPPORTING_EXTERNAL_ENTITIES is FALSE. Rejected as a lead: external entity expansion (XXE) appears blocked, so the residual concern is entity-expansion DoS only, and no clear injection/revert evidence was found.
rejected_leads.reason: Not a concrete exploitable issue on the evidence available; main XXE vector appears blocked.

rejected_leads.lead: FreeMarkerUtil disables its template cache unconditionally (services/src/main/java/org/keycloak/theme/FreeMarkerUtil.java line 54, `cache = null;`). Rejected: this is a functional/caching quirk with no demonstrated confidentiality/integrity impact.

Grep-level candidates for injection sinks elsewhere (Runtime.exec/ProcessBuilder, ObjectInputStream, native SQL concatenation, XML parser factories without hardening) were checked; the only occurrences are test utilities or fixed/parameterized code, so no candidate was formed.
rejected_leads.reason: No attacker-controlled data flow to these sinks was found.

summary: Reviewed the Keycloak 4.6.0.Final-SNAPSHOT source snapshot (5,108 visible files; no precomputed relation index in this B0 run). The strongest source-evidenced issue found is a server-side request forgery (blind SSRF) in the OIDC authorization endpoint: the unauthenticated `request_uri` authorization-request parameter is fetched directly through the server's outbound HTTP client without any scheme/host/allow-list validation, and the fetched body is read unbounded into memory. Other security-sensitive areas I traced (SAML DOM/Signature validation and the assertion-mixing check, redirect-URI validation, token verification/client binding, PBKDF2 password hashing, admin permission evaluators) appear to contain their expected protections; those leads are listed as rejected. One candidate is submitted; it is a lead, not a confirmed vulnerability.
